text:
AUGUSTA, Ga. (WJBF) — As questions continue surrounding the future of Dwight D. Eisenhower Army Medical Center, one military retiree is sharing his recent experience, saying it has left him worried about what proposed changes could mean for thousands of patients who rely on the hospital.

The Defense Health Agency plans to transition Eisenhower Army Medical Center into an outpatient-focused facility, eliminating inpatient services. The proposal has drawn opposition from Georgia's congressional delegation, including Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, who have urged the agency to abandon the plan.

Hal Doyle, a retired Air Force veteran, said his concerns became personal after he went to Eisenhower's emergency department with chest pains earlier this month.

Doyle said doctors determined he needed to stay overnight for additional monitoring and testing, but he was transferred to another hospital to receive that care.

Following his hospital stay, Doyle said he also encountered questions about his future healthcare while trying to resolve a TRICARE issue.

He shared paperwork with NewsChannel 6, including discharge records, transfer documents and a letter involving his TRICARE coverage. Doyle said he was told during a visit to resolve the issue that he would eventually need to find a new primary care provider once the hospital's transition is complete.

NewsChannel 6 has not independently confirmed that information with the Defense Health Agency.

Doyle said he decided to speak publicly because he believes other military retirees deserve answers about what the future of healthcare at Eisenhower will look like.

"I'm just concerned for my own health care, but for as many other retirees in the area," Doyle said.

Doyle also questioned whether staffing shortages are already affecting patient care, saying he has seen a decline in the number of specialists available over the years.

The Defense Health Agency has said nearby civilian hospitals will help provide inpatient care if the transition moves forward.

NewsChannel 6 reached out to the Defense Health Agency for comment on Doyle's concerns and to ask whether any changes have been made to the proposed transition. As of publication, the agency had not responded.

Congressman Rick Allen's office also told NewsChannel 6 he was unavailable for an interview Tuesday but expects to speak about the issue later this week.

Georgia lawmakers continue urging the Defense Health Agency to reconsider the proposed changes, saying they are concerned about the potential impact on service members, military retirees, veterans and their families who depend on Eisenhower Army Medical Center.

text:
Naloxone prescriptions reduced emergency department use among individuals at high risk of opioid overdose.

Background

Despite a decrease in opioid prescribing in recent years, opioid overdose deaths remain high. Naloxone is an effective method to reverse opioid overdoses and can be administered in various settings by providers and individuals with no clinical training. This study measured the impact of co-prescribing naloxone to high-risk patients in the Military Health System on visits to the emergency department (ED).

Findings

Health system claims were used to compare ED visit rates among individuals who were dispensed naloxone alongside an opioid prescription versus those who only received opioids. Individuals were classified as high risk if they had long-term opioid use, high prescription dosages, or a history of overdose or behavioral health diagnosis. Individuals in the naloxone group had a 26% reduction in ED visits within 60 days of receiving their prescriptions. Hospitalization rates were also measured between the two groups, but there was no significant difference.

Program/Policy Takeaways

Dispensing naloxone alongside opioid prescriptions can help reduce ED visits among individuals at high risk of overdose. Providers and health systems can use these findings to identify opportunities to screen individuals for overdose risk factors and incorporate naloxone co-prescribing into clinical workflows.

title: From MOAA's President: Help Bring Our Message Home to Lawmakers
description:
Lawmakers will spend most of August away from the nation’s capital.
[REGISTER NOW: MOAA’s Legislative Action Center] This year, we’ve selected three issues: Supporting combat-injured veterans: After years of work by MOAA and other veterans’ advocacy groups, the Major Richard Star Act has made remarkable progress.
But their work, and that of MOAA’s advocacy team in their daily duties, becomes more impactful when the support of 350,000-plus members can be heard loud and clear.
That’s why we are asking you to write to your lawmakers over the summer recess, to call their offices, and to visit them during this preelection work period.
As always, thank you for supporting our advocacy efforts — one of the many ways MOAA members never stop serving.
text:
(This article originally appeared in the August 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

Lawmakers will spend most of August away from the nation’s capital. But while the halls of power might be a little less crowded, lawmakers will be busy in their home states and districts, meeting with constituents just a few weeks before many will stand for election.

And that’s why MOAA needs your voice now.

Our Summer Advocacy in Action campaign will show House and Senate members that the issues core to the uniformed services and veteran communities reach well beyond the Beltway — they make a difference in the lives of voters, and they must be priorities when the 119th Congress reconvenes.

[REGISTER NOW: MOAA’s Legislative Action Center]

This year, we’ve selected three issues:

Supporting combat-injured veterans: After years of work by MOAA and other veterans’ advocacy groups, the Major Richard Star Act has made remarkable progress. But if the 119th Congress can’t pass the legislation — either on its own or as part of a larger bill — we start from scratch in January.

That’s simply an unacceptable outcome for the 59,000 combat-disabled men and women who lose a dollar of earned retirement pay for every dollar of VA disability compensation.

[TAKE ACTION: Advocate for the Major Richard Star Act]

Expanding employment opportunities for veterans and military spouses: Adding veterans to the Work Opportunity Tax Credit helped address an unemployment crisis a decade ago; now, the veteran jobless rate regularly lands lower than that of the overall U.S. population. The credit offers businesses a financial incentive to employ populations that face significant barriers to employment, but it expired at the end of 2025 and hasn’t been renewed.

The bipartisan Improve and Enhance the Work Opportunity Tax Credit Act would do just what it says by not only restoring the incentive but also by adding military spouses to the list of groups that could get a much-needed leg up.

[TAKE ACTION: Ask Your Lawmakers to Support the Improve and Enhance the Work Opportunity Tax Credit Act]

Restoring pharmacy coverage parity for TRICARE For Life beneficiaries: MOAA continues its efforts to reverse an August 2025 Pentagon decision to revoke coverage of certain GLP-1 drugs under TRICARE For Life. This sets a dangerous precedent, weakening a service-earned benefit by establishing a two-tier coverage system.

This is simply not the world-class care many earned via decades in uniform; Congress must use its oversight power to correct this misstep.

[TAKE ACTION: Reinstate TRICARE for Life Coverage of GLP-1 Medications]

Our April Advocacy in Action event on the Hill always reminds me of the dedication of our nationwide network of council and chapter leaders, some of whom traveled thousands of miles to bring our advocacy priorities to the offices of hundreds of lawmakers.

But their work, and that of MOAA’s advocacy team in their daily duties, becomes more impactful when the support of 350,000-plus members can be heard loud and clear.

That’s why we are asking you to write to your lawmakers over the summer recess, to call their offices, and to visit them during this preelection work period. Make sure they understand these three issues aren’t just talking points — they are critical to their constituents, to their communities, and to their reelection.

As always, thank you for supporting our advocacy efforts — one of the many ways MOAA members never stop serving.

(This article originally appeared in the August 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

Capt. M.J. Hessert serves in the Operational Readiness Directorate at the Naval Health Research Center, supporting research focused on physiology, human performance, and medical modeling of conflict and operational health care.

Her Navy career has taken her around the world — from combat zones to aircraft carriers — caring for servicemembers and leading under pressure.

An Unexpected Path

“I joined the Navy through the Health Professions Scholarship Program, which paid for medical school,” Hessert said. “I was commissioned in 2001 and entered active duty in 2005. My initial motivation was pragmatic. The military offered strong educational benefits.

“What has surprised me the most about military service? How long I’ve stayed.”

The Best and Worst of Times

“Much like Charles Dickens described, the highlights of my career have often been the best and worst moments simultaneously. My deployments included flying combat missions in Iraq, saving hundreds of lives in Afghanistan, working with elite units in North Africa, and serving as a senior medical officer aboard an aircraft carrier in the South China Sea. These experiences were both deeply challenging and profoundly memorable.”

Leading by Example

“Like most physicians, I want to help people. My patients happen to be servicemembers and their families, and retirees. I also hope my career demonstrates that women can succeed in traditionally male institutions, even when the path includes persistent obstacles.

“People serve for many different reasons. For some, it’s patriotism or family tradition. For others, it’s access to health care or education. The military can be a meaningful onramp to adulthood and professional growth.”

text:
(This article originally appeared in the August 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

Air travel can test even the most patient person.

Thinking about crowded security lines, flight delays, and lost luggage might be enough to stress you out.

For military families, the stress is often amplified. Tight timelines, multiple bags, traveling with children, and connections can turn a routine trip into a logistical exercise worthy of a military operation.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) is trying to make things easier. In July 2025, the TSA announced its “Serve with Honor, Travel with Ease” initiative, which offers benefits and services specifically designed for servicemembers, veterans, military families, and Gold Star families.

Free TSA PreCheck

Active duty servicemembers can access TSA PreCheck lanes at no cost by using their military ID number as their Known Traveler Number when booking flights. This means shorter lines, keeping shoes on, and laptops staying in their bags.

Military families benefit as well. Children 12 and under may accompany a TSA PreCheck-eligible parent. Travelers ages 13-17 can also receive expedited screening when traveling on the same airline reservation as their eligible parent or guardian.

Dedicated Honor Lanes

At select airports, travelers might also notice dedicated military screening lanes, often referred to as Honor Lanes. Unlike TSA PreCheck, which is a trusted traveler program, Honor Lanes are designated screening areas that help eligible travelers move through security more efficiently while recognizing their service to the nation.

Travelers will still undergo standard TSA screening procedures, but the dedicated lanes can help reduce wait times and streamline the checkpoint experience.

[RELATED: Some Disabled Veterans Qualify for Free TSA PreCheck]

The program is designed for a broad segment of the military community, including active duty servicemembers, military retirees, veterans, military spouses, dependents, and Gold Star families.

These lanes are currently available at:

Austin-Bergstrom International Airport

Charlotte Douglas International Airport

Colorado Springs Airport

Denver International Airport

El Paso International Airport

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport

Nashville International Airport

San Antonio International Airport

San Diego International Airport

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport

Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport

Many of these airports are located near major military installations or serve large military populations. While the lanes might vary by airport, the goal is the same: to help military travelers move through security more efficiently.

Additional Support

For veterans and wounded warriors who might need additional assistance while traveling, the TSA Cares program provides personalized support through the screening process.

The program is designed to help travelers with disabilities, injuries, medical conditions, or other circumstances requiring additional support. If interested, contact the TSA at least 72 hours prior to travel by going online or calling (855) 787-2227.

While these programs won’t completely eliminate the chaos that can come with air travel, they can make it a little more manageable. For a community that spends a lifetime answering the call to go wherever they’re needed, these are small benefits worth knowing before your next trip.

text:
SANFORD, N.C. (WTVD) -- A Sanford speech therapist says a years-long fight with an insurance company over nearly $14,000 in medical claims is finally over, but she says the ordeal ultimately led her to close her practice.

Jeanine Morton, owner of Theraplay NC, says she first learned in 2024 that Humana Military was seeking to recoup $13,930 for more than 130 claims dating back to 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Morton, the claims had originally been paid, but she was later told they needed a Telehealth modifier because the services were provided virtually. Morton says, "Once I was informed, I corrected the claims, mailed and faxed them multiple times every 30 days. I would check on the process. Hey, did you receive these claims? No, we haven't received them. Go ahead and mail them again."

Despite those efforts, she says Humana Military began taking back the money. "It's caused so much stress in my life. It has. It's hard to balance, planning sessions for my kids, being creative and then having to pull time away from my day to work on this every single day," Morton said to ABC11 Troubleshooter Diane Wilson.

Feeling out of options, Morton contacted ABC11 Troubleshooter for help.

After Wilson reached out to Humana Military, Morton says she received a call the next day acknowledging that her corrected claims had been received.

In a statement, Humana Military said:

"The Humana Military team is working with Ms. Morton to resolve her concerns quickly and accurately and acknowledges the frustration that she has experienced. We remain committed to providing excellent care for TRICARE East beneficiaries and the providers who serve them."

After several weeks of additional communication, the dispute was resolved. Morton says Humana Military reimbursed her for the money it had recouped and confirmed she does not owe anything on the claims from 2020.

"Thank you, Diane, for your efforts and your work." While grateful for the outcome, Morton says the prolonged battle took a significant emotional and financial toll. She has since made the difficult decision to close Theraplay NC.

"This has taken the joy of it. It totally has. Taken the joy. It's burnt me out. I hate this for my families because I have great families and kids that I work with. So, it's actually a season of grieving that I have to close this chapter and move," Morton said.

Morton hopes sharing her story encourages other healthcare providers to keep detailed records, save copies of all correspondence, and continue advocating for themselves when billing disputes arise.

text:
What seems like a simple step to prevent financial fraud could instead give bad actors easy access to your bank accounts, credit cards, and other critical personal data.

State and federal resources point to credit monitoring scams as a threat to active duty servicemembers, though similar “protection” schemes may target veterans, military families, or other service-connected individuals.

The process:

A scammer will use news reports, social media posts, or other public information to find a servicemember preparing for deployment, a veteran receiving a new or updated federal benefit, or any other ripe target.

The scammer will reach out via email, text, social media, or phone representing themselves as a credit-monitoring firm – either one of the three established credit reporting agencies or a fake security firm, possibly with a name implying a government or military connection.

As part of “monitoring services,” the scammer requests some level of personal information, such as credit card or bank account information.

With the information secured (and the victim possibly on deployment), scammers use the data to make credit card purchases or secure loans in the victim’s name.

[RELATED: Scam and Fraud Prevention Resources From MOAA]

Staying Safe

Basic scam-awareness and -avoidance tactics can prevent consumers from falling for monitoring schemes. Legitimate credit-monitoring agencies won’t reach out unprompted and won’t communicate via social media or text messages. Always research any such agency via reputable resources, and use official company websites and contact details to reach out with questions instead of replying to texts or clicking links in an email.

Those seeing legitimate credit monitoring services have several choices available, including credit freezes and fraud alerts. Learn more about those products from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

Servicemembers have even more options, including an active duty fraud alert that requires credit bureaus to contact you before opening any accounts in your name and removes you from marketing lists for credit and insurance products. The alert lasts a year and can be renewed.

[RELATED: How to Avoid a Benefits Buyout Scam]

To set up an alert, reach out to any one of the three credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion). Whichever bureau receives the request must forward it to the other two.

text:
(Sponsored by PC Matic)

Transitioning from defending the nation to navigating the civilian digital landscape shouldn't mean dropping your guard. Today, cyber threats are more sophisticated than ever, utilizing artificial intelligence to craft hyper-realistic scams and target veterans specifically. However, the discipline and tactical mindset you developed in the military are your greatest assets. By shifting to a prevention-first model, you can secure your digital life before a threat ever breaches your perimeter.

Tip 1: Establish a Digital Perimeter

In the military, operational security (OPSEC) is second nature. Apply that exact same discipline to your online presence. Cybercriminals frequently target veterans with scams tailored to VA benefits, PACT Act claims, or fake job offers.

Preventative Action Tip: Treat personal details like your years of service, discharge details, and banking information as classified intel. Never share credentials to portals like VA.gov with third parties, even if they promise to help expedite a claim. If a request feels like an unauthorized breach of information, shut it down.

Tip 2: Practice 'Verify Before Trust' with AI Threats

Gone are the days of spotting scams by bad grammar or obvious typos alone. Today's hackers use generative AI to mimic official organizations, write flawless emails, and even simulate the voices of trusted colleagues or family members via deepfakes.

Preventative Action Tip: If you receive an urgent request for money, sensitive information, or login access, even if it sounds exactly like your former commander or an official VA rep, you should pause. Hang up or close the message, and verify the request through an official, independent channel. Never use the contact information provided within the suspicious message.

Tip 3: Fortify Your Pocket

Recent data shows that cybercriminals are pivoting hard toward mobile devices. Smishing (SMS phishing) and malicious scam calls have a much higher success rate because we tend to trust our phones more than our computer screens.

Preventative Action Tip: Treat your smartphone like a critical piece of field equipment. Avoid clicking links in text messages from unknown numbers. Turn on spam-blocking features offered by your carrier, and carefully vet apps before downloading them to your device.

Tip 4: Deploy Two-Factor Authentication Everywhere

Think of multifactor authentication (MFA) as a dual-key system for a secure vault. Even if a bad actor manages to compromise your password via a large-scale data breach, they still cannot access your account without that second, physical confirmation.

Preventative Action Tip: Turn on MFA for all critical accounts, especially email, banking, and government portals. When given the choice, opt for an authenticator app over standard SMS texts, as text messages are easier for advanced attackers to intercept.

Tip 5: Keep Your Gear Maintained

You wouldn’t head out on a mission with unmaintained gear. In the cyber realm, outdated software is the equivalent of a rusted weapon. Hackers actively scan for known software vulnerabilities to bypass security measures entirely.

Preventative Action Tip: Do not delay those annoying update notifications. Set your smartphone, computer, and smart home devices to update automatically. These updates regularly patch security holes before hackers can exploit them, serving as your ultimate passive shield.

The Bottom Line

You already possess the situational awareness and strategic discipline required to face modern cyber threats. By focusing on prevention rather than reaction, you deny adversaries the element of surprise.

Stay sharp, verify everything, and keep your digital perimeter secure.

title: Can You Suspend FEHB for TRICARE? Rules for Federal Retirees
description:
‍ Federal retirees, survivor annuitants, and eligible former spouses can suspend FEHB coverage to use TRICARE.
Federal Pension Advisors, a retirement planning firm specializing in federal employee benefits, can help you review how FEHB, TRICARE, and retirement timing may interact.
‍ Why Active Employees Cannot Suspend FEHB ‍ Active federal employees can't suspend FEHB coverage.
‍ How the FEHB Five-Year Rule Interacts With TRICARE ‍ The FEHB five-year rule is the eligibility test that determines whether you can carry FEHB coverage into retirement, and TRICARE coverage can count toward it.
‍ How to Suspend FEHB Coverage as a Retiree ‍ Suspending FEHB as an annuitant requires submitting the correct documentation within a specific window.
text:
‍

Federal retirees, survivor annuitants, and eligible former spouses can suspend FEHB coverage to use TRICARE. Active federal employees cannot.

‍

To suspend FEHB coverage means to pause your enrollment in the Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) Program while you use another form of coverage such as TRICARE, and to keep the right to reinstate FEHB later. Active employees don't have this option. They can only cancel FEHB, which ends the current enrollment and can jeopardize their ability to carry coverage into retirement if they aren't enrolled again by their retirement date.

‍

This distinction is the single most important thing federal workers need to understand before making any change. Getting it wrong can cost you one of the most valuable benefits in federal service.

‍

This guide explains who can suspend FEHB, how suspension differs from cancellation, how the FEHB five-year rule interacts with TRICARE, and how to reinstate your coverage. Federal Pension Advisors, a retirement planning firm specializing in federal employee benefits, can help you review how FEHB, TRICARE, and retirement timing may interact.

‍

What Does It Mean to Suspend FEHB Coverage?

‍

To suspend FEHB coverage is to place your Federal Employees Health Benefits enrollment on hold so you can use non-FEHB coverage, while preserving your right to return to FEHB later. Suspension isn't the same as cancellation.

‍

When you suspend, you stop paying FEHB premiums and stop using FEHB benefits. Your enrollment record stays intact for future reinstatement.

‍

According to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), annuitants and survivors who suspend their enrollment can reenroll in an FEHB plan during a future Open Season, or immediately if they involuntarily lose their non-FEHB coverage (OPM annuitants reference). Suspension can help eligible retirees avoid paying for overlapping health coverage while preserving a path back to FEHB.

‍

Who Can Suspend FEHB to Use TRICARE?

‍

Only annuitants, survivor annuitants, and eligible former spouses can suspend FEHB coverage to use TRICARE or CHAMPVA. According to OPM, these individuals may suspend enrollment to use TRICARE, TRICARE-for-Life, or CHAMPVA instead of FEHB, and can apply to suspend their coverage at any time (OPM guidance on suspending FEHB for TRICARE or CHAMPVA).

‍

Active federal employees are excluded from this option entirely. The right to suspend is a retiree and annuitant benefit, not an employee benefit.

‍

If you're still working in federal service, suspension simply isn't available to you, no matter how good your TRICARE eligibility is.

‍

TRICARE is the health care program for uniformed service members, retirees, and their families administered by the Department of Defense. TRICARE-for-Life is the Medicare-wraparound coverage for TRICARE beneficiaries who are enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B. CHAMPVA, the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs, covers eligible dependents of certain disabled or deceased veterans.

‍

Why Active Employees Cannot Suspend FEHB

‍

Active federal employees can't suspend FEHB coverage. They can only cancel it. According to OPM, employees may not suspend their FEHB coverage, but they can cancel it to use CHAMPVA or certain TRICARE plans (OPM guidance on active employees and FEHB suspension).

‍

This difference matters enormously. Cancellation is a full termination of your enrollment, not a pause.

‍

An employee who cancels FEHB to rely on TRICARE gives up current FEHB enrollment. That employee must be enrolled again in an FEHB plan on the retirement date to carry FEHB into retirement.

‍

There's one important nuance. OPM notes that employees enrolled in premium conversion can't treat TRICARE or CHAMPVA eligibility as a qualifying life event, so those employees may generally only cancel during the annual FEHB Open Season.

‍

Suspend vs. Cancel: The Comparison Every Federal Worker Needs

‍

The difference between suspending and cancelling FEHB is the difference between a protected reinstatement right and losing that protection. The table below sets out how the two actions compare and who is eligible for each.

‍

‍

According to OPM, a federal retiree who suspends FEHB to enroll in TRICARE can reenroll during a future Open Season. An employee who cancels can generally only return during a later Open Season, with no guaranteed protection of retirement eligibility.

‍

Both suspension and cancellation for retirees are documented on OPM's Form RI 79-9, the Health Benefits Cancellation/Suspension Confirmation form, which provides a separate page for each action (OPM Form RI 79-9).

‍

How the FEHB Five-Year Rule Interacts With TRICARE

‍

The FEHB five-year rule is the eligibility test that determines whether you can carry FEHB coverage into retirement, and TRICARE coverage can count toward it. According to OPM, to carry FEHB into retirement you must be entitled to retire on an immediate annuity. You must also have been continuously enrolled in any FEHB plan for the five years of service immediately before your annuity starts, or for the full period since your first opportunity to enroll if that's less than five years.

‍

Time covered under TRICARE counts toward meeting this five-year requirement, as long as you were covered under an FEHB enrollment on the date you retire (OPM healthcare eligibility). You can hold TRICARE during your working years and still satisfy the rule, but you must be enrolled in an FEHB plan on your actual retirement date to preserve the benefit.

‍

This is exactly why cancelling FEHB as an employee is so dangerous. If you cancel and aren't enrolled in FEHB on your retirement date, you lose the ability to carry FEHB into retirement, even if TRICARE covered you for years.

‍

According to OPM, the fix is to stay enrolled in FEHB through your retirement date, then suspend it as a retiree once your annuity begins.

‍

How to Suspend FEHB Coverage as a Retiree

‍

Suspending FEHB as an annuitant requires submitting the correct documentation within a specific window. According to OPM, annuitants can call the Retirement Information Office at 1-888-767-6738 to request a suspension form, or use the online tools at servicesonline.opm.gov. The required form is RI 79-9, the Health Benefits Cancellation/Suspension Confirmation form.

‍

For TRICARE or TRICARE-for-Life, OPM requires a copy of your Uniformed Services Identification card. For those over age 65, you also need a Medicare card showing enrollment in Parts A and B. For CHAMPVA, you must provide a copy of your CHAMPVA Authorization Card (A-card).

‍

Timing matters. According to OPM, you must submit documentation within the period beginning 31 days before and ending 31 days after the date you want the suspension to take effect. If OPM receives your documentation within that window, the suspension takes effect the day before your designated date. Otherwise, it takes effect on the first day of the first pay period after OPM receives it.

‍

How to Reinstate FEHB After Suspension

‍

You can reinstate suspended FEHB coverage during any Open Season, or immediately if you involuntarily lose your TRICARE or CHAMPVA coverage. According to OPM, annuitants and survivors who have suspended their enrollment may reenroll in an FEHB plan during a future Open Season for any reason, or return to FEHB immediately upon an involuntary loss of the non-FEHB coverage.

‍

This two-track reinstatement is the whole point of suspending rather than cancelling. It lets you drop FEHB premiums while TRICARE serves your needs, and it gives you a guaranteed path back if TRICARE stops working for you or your circumstances change.

‍

Voluntarily dropping TRICARE isn't an involuntary loss. A voluntary change generally means waiting for the next Open Season to be reinstated.

‍

A Planning Scenario: Retiring With Both FEHB and TRICARE

‍

Consider a retiring FERS, the Federal Employees Retirement System, employee who is also a military retiree with TRICARE-for-Life. A common mistake would be to cancel FEHB a year or two before retirement to save on premiums, assuming TRICARE will cover everything.

‍

Doing so could leave the retiree unable to carry FEHB into retirement, because they wouldn't have been enrolled in FEHB on the retirement date.

‍

The correct sequence is to stay enrolled in FEHB through the retirement date, retire on an immediate annuity, and then suspend FEHB as an annuitant. That approach stops FEHB premium payments while keeping a protected reinstatement right as a fallback.

‍

Federal Pension Advisors can help you review your FEHB-into-retirement options before you make a change.

‍

The Bottom Line

‍

The rule to remember is simple: don't confuse cancelling FEHB as an employee with suspending FEHB as a retiree. Suspension is a reversible pause available only to annuitants, survivor annuitants, and eligible former spouses, and it lets you use TRICARE while keeping a protected path back to FEHB.

‍

Cancellation ends your current enrollment and can cost you the ability to carry FEHB into retirement if you aren't enrolled again by your retirement date. Because TRICARE coverage counts toward the FEHB five-year rule but you must be enrolled in FEHB on your retirement date, timing your decision correctly is essential.

‍

Federal Pension Advisors, a retirement planning firm specializing in federal employee benefits, can help you review how your FEHB and TRICARE decisions may fit together before you make a change. To review how FEHB and TRICARE may fit into your retirement timing, contact Federal Pension Advisors before making a coverage change.

‍

Frequently Asked Questions

‍

1. Can you suspend FEHB coverage if you have TRICARE?

Yes, if you're an annuitant, survivor annuitant, or eligible former spouse. According to OPM, these individuals may suspend FEHB to use TRICARE, TRICARE-for-Life, or CHAMPVA and can apply to suspend at any time. Active federal employees can't suspend FEHB. They may only cancel it.

‍

2. What is the difference between suspending and cancelling FEHB?

Suspending FEHB pauses your enrollment while preserving your right to reinstate it later. Cancelling FEHB ends your current enrollment. According to OPM, suspended annuitants can reenroll during Open Season or immediately on involuntary loss of other coverage, while cancellation offers no protected reinstatement right and can jeopardize retirement eligibility.

‍

3. Does TRICARE count toward the FEHB five-year rule?

Yes. According to OPM, time covered under TRICARE counts toward the five-year requirement to carry FEHB into retirement, as long as you were enrolled in an FEHB plan on your retirement date. You must hold FEHB on the date you retire to keep the benefit.

‍

4. How do I reinstate FEHB after suspending it for TRICARE?

According to OPM, you can reinstate suspended FEHB during any Open Season for any reason, or immediately if you involuntarily lose your TRICARE or CHAMPVA coverage. You submit documentation to your retirement system, and reinstatement timing depends on when OPM receives it.

‍

5. What form do I use to suspend FEHB as a retiree?

You use Form RI 79-9, the Health Benefits Cancellation/Suspension Confirmation form. According to OPM, TRICARE enrollees must include a copy of their Uniformed Services ID card, plus a Medicare card showing Parts A and B if over age 65, while CHAMPVA enrollees include the CHAMPVA A-card.

‍

6. Can active federal employees drop FEHB to use TRICARE?

Active employees can't suspend FEHB, but according to OPM they may cancel it to use CHAMPVA or certain TRICARE plans. Employees in premium conversion generally can only cancel during Open Season, since TRICARE eligibility isn't a qualifying life event for them.

‍

Disclaimer

This article is for educational purposes only and should not be treated as legal, tax, insurance, financial, or federal benefits advice. FEHB and TRICARE rules can vary based on retirement status, eligibility, enrollment type, military benefits, family coverage, and current OPM or TRICARE guidance. Federal employees and retirees should verify their options with OPM, TRICARE, their agency benefits office, and a qualified federal benefits professional before suspending or changing health coverage.

text: WASHINGTON – A federal jury in the Middle District of Florida has convicted an Oklahoma business owner and chiropractor for his role in a yearslong scheme that attempted to bilk Medicare, TRICARE, and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) out of more than $30 million by purchasing patient information, medical practitioner signatures and doctor orders for orthotic braces and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) that patients did not want or need, according to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). “The defendant turned private medical data into a pipeline for personal profit,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “Every fake doctor’s order generated was a direct attack on systems built to care for some of our nation’s most vulnerable. (This) verdict makes clear that if you exploit our seniors and military families to fill your own pockets, you will answer for every dollar stolen.” According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Mark Loftis, 39, of Cushing, paid more than $1 million to marketers who worked with call centers to persuade elderly and disabled Americans to provide their personal information, including their health insurance information. Loftis and his co-conspirators then used that information to obtain signed orders for orthotic braces and CGMs that were generated by telemedicine doctors and nurse practitioners who never examined, and often never spoke, to the patients. Loftis and his co-conspirators used these orders to bill federal health care programs. Loftis also concealed a conspirator’s management role in his company and his billing of claims generated by other unenrolled medical suppliers. In total, Loftis obtained more than $8 million from the false and fraudulent claims. Loftis continued the scheme for three years despite receiving a steady stream of complaints from beneficiaries and family members of beneficiaries who reported that their elderly parents suffered from dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, making them especially vulnerable to the sales tactics of Loftis’s conspirators. The jury convicted Loftis of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 7, 2026, and faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

title: Barriers to Pediatric Hospice Care
description:
Terminally ill children face barriers to hospice care, often stemming from the emotional toll of making that decision, among other factors.
Nevertheless, pediatric hospice services are growing, according to the National Alliance for Care at Home.
“One of the greatest challenges in pediatric hospice and palliative care is simply awareness,” Florido told Hospice News.
“Many healthcare providers and families are unfamiliar with the full scope of services available or assume these services are only appropriate at the very end of life.” Empath Health networks include Empath Hospice, Hospice of Marion County, Suncoast Hospice, Suncoast Hospice of Hillsborough, Tidewell Hospice and Trustbridge Hospice.
The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) established concurrent care for pediatric patients who have a six-month terminal prognosis.
text:
Terminally ill children face barriers to hospice care, often stemming from the emotional toll of making that decision, among other factors.

Overall data on pediatric hospice utilization are scarce. Less than 10% of terminally ill patients younger than 21-years-old receive hospice care, according to the National Institutes of Health. The American Academy of Pediatrics reports that children account for less than 1% of total hospice patients, despite tens of thousands of annual deaths from life-limiting illnesses.

Nevertheless, pediatric hospice services are growing, according to the National Alliance for Care at Home.

“Pediatric hospice and palliative care in the United States continues to expand in visibility and perceived value, driven by increasing recognition that children with serious illness and their families benefit from early, coordinated symptom management, communication support, psychosocial and spiritual care,” the Alliance indicated in its 2025 Pediatric Facts and Figures Report.

But pediatric patients still encounter roadblocks, according to the Alliance. Chief among these is a lack of pediatric-trained clinicians and infrequent referrals. Inadequate reimbursement and high costs are also factors, among others, the organization reported.

Most pediatric hospice patients receive coverage through Medicaid, private insurance and TRICARE for active military and veterans. Policies and payment rates can vary among these entities.

A lack of awareness also stands in the way of these patients receiving comfort care at the end of life, according to Cristie Florido, director of pediatric programs at the hospice and serious illness care provider Empath Health.

“One of the greatest challenges in pediatric hospice and palliative care is simply awareness,” Florido told Hospice News. “Many healthcare providers and families are unfamiliar with the full scope of services available or assume these services are only appropriate at the very end of life.”

Empath Health networks include Empath Hospice, Hospice of Marion County, Suncoast Hospice, Suncoast Hospice of Hillsborough, Tidewell Hospice and Trustbridge Hospice. Empath Health’s Full Life Care services include hospice, home health, palliative care, grief support and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE), as well as HIV/STI prevention.

The nonprofit’s pediatric programs recently expanded thanks in part to more than a million grant dollars from two foundations and its recent merger with Trustbridge, according to Florido. Its current pediatric census hovers around 61 patients, representing a 100% increase since October 2025.

Many families and potential referring physicians may also not know that pediatric patients younger than 21 are eligible to receive concurrent hospice and curative care, according to Florido.

The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) established concurrent care for pediatric patients who have a six-month terminal prognosis. This applies to children who are enrolled in Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP). TRICARE and many private insurance companies also allow concurrent care.

Another barrier that children face when accessing hospice care is a misconception among families and clinicians in other settings that children are “not supposed to be sick,” Florido indicated.

“There are children living longer and longer with chronic illnesses. But at some point, goals might shift or children might decline,” Florido said. “There’s a misconception that children are not supposed to be sick, but unfortunately this is happening. It’s the reality. So, we’re here to help them through that through that journey, and just walk alongside them through those hardships with them and their family members.”

If possible, visit the pharmacy where the prescription was filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may be filled at another store in that chain. If the clinician who prescribed the medication is available, beneficiaries can ask them to call in a new prescription to any network pharmacy.

As a reminder, TRICARE beneficiaries, other than active duty service members, may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider and do not need a referral. This allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency care for illnesses or injuries if their primary care provider is unavailable because of emergencies. Any TRICARE beneficiary who reasonably believes they have an emergency should always call 911 or, go to the nearest emergency room.

text:
When the military faces a retention crisis among high-value, highly traine personnel, such as Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) technicians and aviation specialists, the diagnosis usually focuses on operational tempo, private sector pay or deployment fatigue. But today, an unexpected and unnecessary driver is forcing elite operators to hand in their uniforms: a broken defense healthcare policy that penalizes their special-needs children.

In May 2026, South Carolina enacted Act 186 with overwhelming bipartisan support. Under an Americans with Disabilities Act framework, the law guarantees that autistic children can receive medically necessary behavioral health support, specifically Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy, inside public-school classrooms.

It was designed to ensure that no child must forfeit their public education to access required medical care.

Yet, active-duty military families stationed at Joint Base Charleston and across the state are being stripped of this protection.

The Defense Health Agency (DHA), operating through TRICARE's Autism Care Demonstration (ACD), continues to enforce a rigid "School Exclusion" rule.

Under this administrative posture, TRICARE completely cuts off provider reimbursement the moment a behavior technician steps onto public school property. While civilian families with commercial insurance benefit from state law protections, military families face an impossible ultimatum: Either pull their children out of public school to maintain therapy in a clinical setting or drop medically necessary care so their children can attend school alongside their peers.

The operational cost of this bureaucratic conflict is staggering.

Summer 2026 field survey data from The Military Family Advocacy Group reveals that 100% of surveyed active-duty, mid-career operators navigating these TRICARE autism denials are actively planning early separation from military service.

When a specialized EOD technician or fighter pilot is consumed by an exhausting administrative war at home just to secure standard healthcare for their child, mission focus fractures and unit lethality suffers. The military spends millions of dollars and years of specialized training to build these operators, only to lose them over a TRICARE setting restriction.

Adding insult to injury is the financial cost-shift onto local taxpayers.

Denied in-school coverage by TRICARE, 80% of surveyed military families have been forced to enroll their dependents onto state-funded Medicaid waivers to cover essential care. This shifts an estimated $6,383 annual net tax burden per child directly onto South Carolina taxpayers for care that a federal defense program should be providing.

This systemic breakdown is not inevitable; it is the result of administrative intransigence.

In 2025, a comprehensive report by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) recommended that the Defense Health Agency discontinue the 12-year ACD "demonstration" status, authorize ABA as a standard TRICARE Basic benefit, remove arbitrary setting exclusions and eliminate onerous assessment mandates.

Because the Defense Health Agency has repeatedly failed to self-correct or adopt these independent scientific recommendations, Congress must step in.

As lawmakers finalize the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, they must include statutory language that legally compels the secretary of defense to terminate the ACD demonstration status, align TRICARE with NASEM standards and prohibit the Defense Health Agency from restricting medically necessary care based on geographic or educational settings.

South Carolina has done its part to protect military children. It is now time for federal lawmakers to enforce those protections, end the school exclusion rule and preserve the readiness of our total force.

Mariah Wilkins is the executive director and principal policy advisor of The Military Family Advocacy Group.

Firefighters were called to 122 W. Glendale Ave. at 1:13 p.m.

Batallion 4 arrived to heavy fire showing from the two-family residence, and started an aggressive attack, Fire Chief Keven Vanegas said.

A dog and cat were rescued from inside the burning home.

text:
San Diego’s congressional delegation is rolling out a one-two punch in Washington to tackle the towering price tag of in vitro fertilization and other fertility treatments. Rep. Sara Jacobs is reviving a bipartisan push to make TRICARE cover infertility care for service members and their dependents, while Rep. Mike Levin is pitching a plan to let people tap retirement savings for fertility costs without getting hit with the usual tax penalty. Supporters say the mix of policies, one focused on insurance and the other on how people pay, could ease the strain, but no one is pretending it solves everything.

What Jacobs' bill would do

Jacobs’ Bipartisan IVF for Military Families Act (H.R. 6797) would change Title 10 of the U.S. Code so that TRICARE must cover fertility treatment, including IVF, for active-duty service members and their dependents. The legislation, introduced on Dec. 17, 2025, has been sent to the House Armed Services Committee, according to GovInfo. Backers say the goal is to ease retention and readiness problems that crop up when military families delay having children or leave the service entirely because they cannot afford fertility care out of pocket.

Levin's financial fix

Rep. Mike Levin’s Fertility Cost Relief Act takes a different tack. The proposal would let individuals pull up to $20,000 from IRAs and 401(k) accounts to pay for qualified fertility treatment without triggering the standard 10% early-withdrawal penalty, according to a press release from Rep. Mike Levin. Levin’s office notes that the idea mirrors existing exceptions for other family-building costs and points to federal estimates showing IVF can cost tens of thousands of dollars for many patients. Supporters argue the change would give families a quicker financing option while they wait for broader insurance reforms that may or may not survive the legislative gauntlet.

State laws help, but gaps remain

California tried to shore up infertility coverage in 2024 when Gov. Gavin Newsom signed SB 729, a measure that compels many large-group plans to cover diagnosis and treatment of infertility, including IVF, according to the Governor's Office. Even so, families still often end up staring down thousands of dollars in deductibles, copays and medication costs, even after the insurance kicks in, according to local reporting and clinic price lists cited by the Times of San Diego. Advocates say that is why federal rules are needed to set a baseline so military households and other patients are not left at the mercy of geography or employer benefits.

TRICARE's rules now

Right now, TRICARE generally does not cover assisted reproductive technology such as IVF, with only narrow exceptions in some service-connected cases or through limited supplemental programs, according to TRICARE. That patchwork means a family’s access and out-of-pocket costs can depend heavily on whether a nearby military treatment facility offers services or whether they have to seek care from civilian providers. Proponents of a statutory mandate say writing the coverage into law would help standardize benefits across the armed forces.

Legislative hurdles and what's next

Lawmakers have tried to tuck similar coverage language into past versions of the National Defense Authorization Act, only to see it stripped out during conference talks, and standalone bills such as H.R. 6797 are still sitting in committee. The Congressional Budget Office has warned that expanding TRICARE coverage for assisted reproductive technology raises questions about discretionary spending and implementation that Congress will need to resolve, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Even with sponsors on both sides of the aisle, the proposals still need committee time, budget clearance and, most likely, a larger legislative vehicle to hitch a ride on before they can become law.

text:
An amendment to codify President Donald Trump’s ban on transgender people serving in the U.S. military according to their gender identity failed to pass as an amendment to Congress’ annual defense bill after two Republicans defected.

Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) proposed the amendment during a flurry of proposed amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act on the House floor on Tuesday evening.

Last month, an appeals court in a 2-1 order struck down the Trump administration’s executive order, calling it fueled by “animus” and the disqualifications listed “completely unexplained and have no reasonable justification.”

The amendment failed 212-217. Reps. Mike Lawler of New York and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris, opposed the amendment.

Republican delegates James Moylan from Guam, and Kimberlyn King-Hinds from the Northern Mariana Islands, also opposed it, though delegates from commonwealths do not get a vote on the final passage of the NDAA.

But Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), the loudly anti-transgender Republican who lost her primary for governor, successfully proposed two anti-trans amendments. One amendment would ban TRICARE, the military health insurance plan, from “covering certain gender related medical procedures and treatments.”

Five Democrats would join Republicans to pass the amendment 219-208: Reps. Shomari Figures of Alabama, Terri Sewell of Alabama, Henry Cuellar of Texas, Don Davis of North Carolina and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas. Davis, Cuellar and Gonzalez all represent districts that voted for Trump while Republicans plan to redraw their congressional map in Alabama, which could put Figures at risk.

Another amendment by Mace would prohibit transgender people assigned male at birth from participating in women’s K-12 sports at Department of Defense-run schools. That amendment would also pass 221-203 with Davis, Gonzalez, Cuelar, Sewell and Figures voting for it.

“Both of my NDAA amendments targeting mentally ill transgenders — and protecting our women and girls — passed the floor of the U.S. House of Representatives tonight with flying colors,” Mace said on social media.

Mace, a member of the Armed Services Committee, had made anti-trans policy a hallmark of her third term in Congress as she teed up a run for governor. But she would place fifth last month in the Republican primary. She also passed on running for the Senate seat of the late Lindsey Graham.

The NDAA sets national defense policy and has often been one of the only successful avenues for Republicans to successfully pass anti-trans provisions. In 2024, House Republicans inserted an amendment to ban TRICARE from covering “certain medical procedures for children that could result in sterilization.” The legislation eventually passed.

In 2025, Republicans successfully inserted an amendment that prohibited transgender athletes from participating in sports designated for women and girls at the United States Military Academy, the U.S. Naval Academy and the U.S. Air Force Academy.

The Senate has yet to pass its version of the NDAA for the fiscal year of 2027. In the past, Democrats have been able to strip some amendments from the NDAA because of the fact it needs 60 votes to pass.

The Senate Armed Services Committee has already completed its markup. If it passes, the two chambers will go to conference to negotiate a final version of the legislation.
